newsitem.title: LEBANON: Pope on delicate mission to Lebanon Christians.
newsitem.headline: Pope on delicate mission to Lebanon Christians.

text.p: Church bells will ring out across Lebanon on Saturday to greet Pope John Paul when he arrives on a brief but delicate mission to help Lebanon's divided Christians find a role in the postwar life of their country.
The 32-hour visit from noon (0900 GMT) on Saturday to seven p.m. (1600 GMT) on Sunday will be John Paul's first trip to the Middle East in his much-travelled papacy.
It is also the first by a pope to the region in more than 30 years -- since Paul VI visited the Holy Land in 1964 and stopped at Beirut airport on his way to Bombay later that year.

The visit is a huge event for Lebanon's Christian minority which emerged defeated and divided from the 1975-90 civil war and has largely refused to reconcile itself to the Syrian-dominated government which many see as undermining their country's independence.

Despite concern about what the pope may have to say, most Moslem clerics and politicians have welcomed the visit and Sunni Moslem Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri has said he is proud the pope has chosen Lebanon for his first Middle East trip.
The government, which is divided equally between pro-Syrian Moslems and Christians but excludes nationalist Christians, has decked Beirut with flags of welcome.

In a country that was a by-word for mayhem in the 1980s, it has mounted a massive security operation to guard the pope with 25,000 soldiers and security troops backed by sniffer dogs, navy patrol boats and helicopters.

Lebanon's Christians, who dominated the small, mountainous country before the war, have looked for centuries to Rome and the West for moral and political support and they are hoping John Paul will now strengthen their hand.
The big question is whether he will repeat a call for the withdrawal of Syrian and Israeli troops from Lebanon that was issued by a Synod of the Lebanese Church in Rome in 1995.

The Church, led by Maronite Patriarch Cardinal Nasrallah Sfeir, has become the main postwar spokesman for the bitterness many Christians and some Moslems feel at the presence of 35,000 Syrian troops in their country and at the authorities' perceived surrender of Lebanon's decision-making powers to Syria.
Big crowds, eager to hear what the pope's message will be, are expected to greet John Paul at a Saturday meeting with young Christians and a Sunday mass on the Beirut seafront.

"I have no doubt this will be a very big event for Christians and they will try to release their frustrations through this visit," Michael Young of the Lebanese Centre for Policy Studies, a Beirut think-tank, told Reuters.

"The question is whether the Maronite church can channel these energies into a new message to unite Lebanese Christians. They are divided and they haven't defined themselves in the postwar republic, and this is bad for Lebanon," Young said.

Vatican officials say the pope is attached to Lebanon as the only Arab country in which all citizens -- Moslem and Christian alike -- are treated as equals thanks to its traditions of freedom of thought, expression and association -- and he wants it to be a source of inspiration in the Middle East.
That means he wants to show that Christians are comfortable in their country and can be trusted to play a positive role in its life.
But analysts believe the pope will have a tough time convincing the Christians to become more integrated.
"The problem is that Lebanese political life is so clearly dominated by Syria, so the Vatican doesn't want to be on record as supporting the status quo," Young said.

"So I think the pope will emphasise the independence of Lebanon and the need for the withdrawal of foreign forces. I think he will come out strongly emphasising the need for Lebanese independence," he added.
John Paul will meet Moslem clerics and politicians. Many curious Moslems, sensing that the visit is an historic event, are expected to mingle with the Sunday worshippers at mass.
The pope's main message will be contained in an Apostolic Exhortation, a document summing up the conclusions of the December 1995 synod, on Sunday.
The question all Lebanese are asking is whether it will differ from the hard-hitting conclusions the synod issued at the time which caused an uproar among Moslems.

The synod said the Lebanese were demoralised by feeling they were not masters in their own country and urged politicians to assume their responsibility for safeguarding its independence and freedom of decision.
And it bluntly demanded the withdrawal of both Syrian and Israeli troops from Lebanon, as well as an end to arbitrary arrests, torture and political imprisonments.
